turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's the difference between a latte and a flat white?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A flat white has less milk and a thinner layer of foam, so it tastes stronger. A latte is bigger and milkier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And a cappuccino?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A cappuccino has a thick layer of foam on top, and it's usually smaller than a latte.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So if I want something / not too milky but still creamy?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A flat white is probably your best bet. Strong coffee flavour with a smooth, velvety texture.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'm going to order one tomorrow and see.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Enjoy it. If it's too strong, you can always ask for an extra splash of milk.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My coffee from the drip machine always tastes bitter. What am I doing wrong?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A few things can cause that. Are you using pre-ground coffee, and how long does it sit on the hot plate?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Pre-ground, and it sits there most of the morning.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's likely it. The hot plate keeps cooking the coffee, which makes it bitter. Try pouring it into a thermos right after brewing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, I'd never have guessed that. Anything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Clean the machine with vinegar every month or so. Old oils and scale build up and taste awful.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't think I've ever / descaled it, to be honest.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you'll probably notice a big difference. Run a couple of rounds of plain water afterwards to rinse it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How late in the day can I drink coffee and still sleep?

turns.text: Caffeine stays in your system for quite a while, about half of it is still there five or six hours later. Many people stop around early afternoon.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So no coffee after lunch?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you go to bed around eleven, try to have your last cup by about two. Everyone's a bit different though.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about decaf? Is that / totally caffeine free?

turns.text: I want to make iced coffee at home this summer. Where do I start?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The easiest way is to brew your coffee a bit stronger than usual and pour it over lots of ice, so it doesn't get watery.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about cold brew? Is that hard?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's really easy, just slow. Mix coarse coffee with cold water, leave it in the fridge overnight, and strain it in the morning.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long does it keep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About a week in the fridge. Make a big jar on Sunday and you're set for the week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Actually, maybe I'll / try both and see which I like.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good idea. Freeze some coffee in an ice cube tray too, so your drink never gets diluted.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My espresso shots taste really sour, and they come out in like ten seconds.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a classic sign of the grind being too coarse. Water rushes through without pulling out enough flavour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So, finer?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, a little finer at a time. You're aiming for roughly twenty five to thirty seconds for a standard shot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if it starts / dripping really slowly?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you've gone too fine, and it'll taste bitter. Somewhere in the middle is the sweet spot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much coffee should I put in?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Weigh it if you can. Keep the dose the same each time and only change the grind, so you know what's making the difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I just found out I'm pregnant. Do I have to give up coffee completely?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Congratulations! Many health guidelines say a moderate amount is okay, often up to about two hundred milligrams of caffeine a day. Your doctor or midwife can tell you what's right for you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much coffee is that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Roughly one or two regular cups, depending on how strong they are. A big cafe coffee can have quite a lot more than one made at home.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about / tea and chocolate?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Those count too, though they usually have less. It's the total across the day that matters.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Decaf is fine, then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Decaf has very little caffeine, so it's a nice way to keep the ritual. Just check with your midwife if you have any doubts.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm in a hotel room with just a kettle and some sad instant sachets. Any way to make decent coffee?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little creativity helps. If you have ground coffee, you can make cowboy style coffee in a mug.

turns.text: I could grab some ground coffee from the shop downstairs. How does that work?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put a spoonful or two in a mug, pour hot water just off the boil, stir, and wait about four minutes. Then let the grounds sink to the bottom.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Won't I drink / a mouthful of grit?

turns.text: A tiny bit, maybe. A splash of cold water on top helps the grounds settle. Pour slowly into a second cup if you have one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Genius. Better than the sachets anyway.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Much better. Some shops also sell single serve drip bags that hang on the mug, perfect for travelling.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a fancy new cafe near me, and the menu is so complicated I just ordered a tea last time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Totally understandable, those menus can be a lot. What kind of coffee do you usually like at home?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Milky, not too strong.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then a latte or a cortado in a bigger size would be safe. Or just tell the barista exactly that, milky and not too strong.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Won't they / judge me for not knowing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most baristas love helping people find something they like. Asking for a recommendation is the best thing you can do.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What's a cortado anyway?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's espresso with a roughly equal amount of warm milk. Smaller and stronger than a latte, so maybe start with the latte.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm vegan and I want a plant milk that actually foams for cappuccinos.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Oat milk is usually the winner. Look for barista versions, they add a bit of fat so it froths like dairy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I tried regular oat milk and it went flat.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's very common with the regular kind. The barista ones hold the foam much better and don't split in hot coffee.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about soy? / Is soy any good?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Soy foams well too, and some people prefer its creamier texture. Almond is the trickiest, it tends to make big bubbles that collapse quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I heat it as hot as dairy milk?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A bit less hot, actually. Plant milks taste best and foam best when they're warm but not scalding.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Coffee keeps upsetting my stomach, but I really don't want to quit.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's frustrating. Do you usually drink it on an empty stomach, first thing in the morning?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yep. Before breakfast, always.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That might be part of it. Try having it with or after some food, even a piece of toast can help a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are some coffees / easier on the stomach?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many people find darker roasts or cold brew gentler. Cold brew tends to taste less acidic, and dark roasts are often softer on the stomach.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I drink about four cups a day, too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Cutting down to two might help as well. If it keeps bothering you, it's worth mentioning to a doctor.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My flatmate keeps our coffee beans in the freezer. Is that right? It seems weird.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a common debate. For beans you'll use within a couple of weeks, an airtight container in a cool, dark cupboard is best.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So the freezer is wrong?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not wrong, just not needed for everyday beans. Taking them in and out of the freezer causes condensation, which isn't great for flavour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: When would freezing / make sense?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you buy a big bag and won't use it for a month or more. Freeze it in small portions and only take out what you need.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. I'll negotiate with him.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Diplomacy is key. And keep them away from the fridge, beans soak up smells like onions surprisingly fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hand grinder or electric grinder? I only make one cup a day.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For one cup, a good hand grinder is great value. You get a consistent grind for much less money than a similar electric one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long does it take to grind by hand?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually somewhere between thirty seconds and a minute for one cup, depending on how fine you go.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's fine for filter, but / what about espresso?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Espresso takes longer by hand because it's very fine. Some people find it a nice morning ritual, others find it tiring.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm not exactly a morning person.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then an electric burr grinder might be worth the extra. Just avoid blade grinders, they chop the beans unevenly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why does my coffee taste different at my parents' house? Same beans, same press.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The water is probably the difference. Hard water, with lots of minerals, can make coffee taste flat or chalky.

turns.text: Their kettle is full of white crust.

turns.text: That's a sure sign of hard water. You could try filtered water there, or a bottle of still water, and compare.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is soft water / always better then?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not always. Water with almost no minerals can make coffee taste thin and sour. Something in the middle is ideal.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh. I never thought water mattered.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's most of what's in your cup, so it matters a lot. Fresh cold water and a clean kettle make a real difference.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm helping with refreshments after my uncle's funeral. We need coffee for about sixty people in the church hall.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'm sorry for your loss. That's a kind thing to take on. Does the hall have a big hot water urn or a catering coffee machine?

turns.text: There's an urn. And some large flasks.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then the simplest way is brewing big batches of filter coffee or using cafetieres and decanting into the flasks. Roughly two tablespoons of ground coffee per mug.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I worry about / people who want decaf?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, it's thoughtful to have one flask of decaf, clearly labelled. Many older guests prefer it in the afternoon.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What else should go on the table?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Milk, sugar, stirrers and maybe a plant milk. And ask someone to keep an eye on the flasks so they never run empty.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want a quick, fancy dessert tonight. I've got coffee and vanilla ice cream.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you're one step from an affogato. It's a scoop of ice cream with a hot shot of espresso poured over it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's it? That's the whole recipe?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's it. Pour it at the table so everyone sees it melt. It looks impressive and takes two minutes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't have an espresso / machine, though.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use very strong coffee from a moka pot or a French press. It won't be quite the same, but it'll still be delicious.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I add something?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A little grated dark chocolate or a crushed biscuit on top is lovely. Some adults add a splash of nut liqueur.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My Turkish neighbour made me coffee in a little pot and it was amazing. Can I make it at home?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can. You'll want a small long handled pot, very finely ground coffee, almost like powder, and cold water.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I need special coffee?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many shops sell coffee ground specifically for it. Regular coffee ground on the finest setting can work if your grinder goes that fine.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And sugar? She asked me / how sweet I wanted it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's because the sugar goes in at the start. You mix coffee, sugar and water in the pot, then heat it slowly without boiling.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I know when it's done?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: When a thick foam rises up to the top, take it off the heat just before it boils over. Pour gently to keep the foam, and let the grounds settle before sipping.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: First shift as a barista tomorrow. I'm terrified of steaming milk wrong in front of customers.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Everyone starts there. The main thing is to start with the steam wand tip just under the surface, so you hear a gentle tearing sound.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Like paper ripping?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly like that. That's air going in. After a few seconds, lower the jug a little so the milk spins like a whirlpool.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And how do I know / when it's hot enough?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Put your hand on the side of the jug. When it's too hot to hold for more than a second or two, it's ready. Some cafes use a thermometer too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if it screams?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the tip being too high or too deep. Adjust slowly. And ask your colleagues for help, nobody expects you to be perfect on day one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I quit coffee three days ago and my head is killing me. Is this normal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very normal, sadly. Caffeine withdrawal headaches usually peak in the first couple of days and fade within about a week.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A week? I can't function like this.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Going cold turkey is the hardest way. Many people find it easier to cut down slowly, like half a cup less every few days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So I could / have a small one now?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You could, and it would probably ease the headache. Then taper down more gently from there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything else that helps?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Drink plenty of water, get some fresh air, and try to sleep a bit more. Your energy usually comes back within a couple of weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I made cold brew concentrate and I have no idea how much to dilute it. My first glass nearly launched me into orbit.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Concentrate is strong stuff, yes. What ratio of coffee to water did you use when you made it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: About one cup of grounds to four cups of water.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a typical concentrate. Try mixing it about half and half with water or milk, then adjust to taste.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Half and half. And with ice / it'll get weaker anyway?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Right, the ice melts a bit and softens it. Some people make coffee ice cubes from leftover cold brew so the drink stays strong.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long will the jar last in the fridge?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Concentrate keeps for about two weeks if it's sealed. Diluted, it's best within a few days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My fifteen year old wants to start drinking coffee like her friends. Should I let her?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many health guidelines say small amounts are okay for teenagers, but recommend limiting caffeine. The bigger concern is usually sleep.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She already stays up way too late.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then the timing matters most. A small coffee in the morning is very different from an iced coffee after school.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Those sweet frappe drinks are / what she really wants.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Those are often more sugar than coffee, so they're more of a dessert. Maybe agree they're an occasional treat, not a daily thing.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That feels like a fair deal.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It sounds reasonable. Letting her try it with some ground rules usually works better than a total ban.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The steam wand on our espresso machine smells funky. Like old milk.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's milk getting sucked up inside the wand and going off. Luckily it's easy to fix.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I clean inside it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Soak the tip in a cup of hot water with a little milk system cleaner, then purge steam through it a few times. Wipe the outside too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a little / hole that seems blocked.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Use a pin or the small tool that came with the machine to gently clear it. Some tips unscrew so you can soak them properly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I stop it happening again?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: After every use, wipe the wand with a damp cloth and blast a short burst of steam. Two seconds of habit saves a lot of smell.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why do coffees from different countries taste so different? I thought coffee was coffee.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a bit like wine. The type of plant, the soil, the altitude and the climate all shape the flavour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So what does Ethiopian taste like compared to, say, Brazilian?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ethiopian coffees are often bright and fruity, sometimes floral. Brazilian ones tend to be nutty and chocolatey, with less acidity.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And Colombian?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Usually balanced, a little sweet, medium body. Many people find it a great everyday coffee.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does how it's processed / matter too?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Hugely. Natural process coffees, dried with the fruit still on, taste fruitier. Washed coffees taste cleaner and crisper.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I should do a tasting at home.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a fun idea. Brew a few side by side the same way, and you'll really notice the differences.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do they even get the caffeine out of decaf? Is it chemicals?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sometimes, but not always. There are a few methods. One uses only water, soaking the green beans and filtering the caffeine out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Only water? That's it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Water and a special carbon filter. Another method uses carbon dioxide under pressure. And some use solvents that are mostly removed afterwards.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Which one / tastes best?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Taste depends more on the beans and roasting, but many people like the water and carbon dioxide processed ones. The bag often says which method was used.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always thought decaf tasted like cardboard.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It used to, often. Good decaf today can be really delicious. Try one from a specialty roaster, you might be surprised.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm throwing a little winter party and I want a cosy spiced coffee. Ideas?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely. You could brew a big pot of coffee with a cinnamon stick, a few cardamom pods and a strip of orange peel.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do I put the spices in the coffee grounds?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You can mix ground cinnamon into the grounds, or simmer whole spices in milk and pour the coffee into it. Simmering gives a gentler, rounder flavour.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I sweeten it / or let people choose?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: I'd keep the coffee unsweetened and put out honey or brown sugar. People's tastes vary a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Could I make it ahead?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Brew the spiced milk ahead and keep it warm in a slow cooker. Add fresh coffee as guests arrive so it doesn't taste stewed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I own a small cafe and I want to add a new seasonal drink. How do I price it without scaring people off?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start by working out the cost of each ingredient per cup, including the milk, syrup and even the cup and lid.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, that's maybe a third of what I'd charge.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a healthy range for drinks. Many cafes aim for ingredients to be roughly a quarter to a third of the price.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But if it's / way more than a latte, will people buy it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Seasonal drinks can usually carry a small premium, because they feel special. Keep it close to your other specialty drinks so it doesn't stick out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I do a taster day?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Great idea. Little sample cups at the counter get people curious, and you'll get honest feedback before committing to a big batch of syrup.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My commute is an hour and a half and my coffee is cold by the time I'm halfway.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a long trip. A vacuum insulated travel mug makes a big difference, the good ones keep coffee hot for hours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mine says it's insulated, but it's useless.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Some cheaper ones only have a single wall. Look for double walled stainless steel and a lid that seals properly. A lot of heat escapes through the lid.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is there a trick / to make it last longer?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, warm the mug first by filling it with hot water for a minute, then pour that out and add your coffee. It stops the cold metal stealing heat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And leak proof? It's going in my bag.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then check the lid locks closed. Some reviews test them upside down in a bag, worth reading before you buy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have a huge bag of used coffee grounds every week. Seems a shame to bin them.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You're right, they're surprisingly useful. Many people add them to compost, they break down nicely.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've heard you can put them / straight on plants.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: In small amounts, mixed into the soil. Too much in a thick layer can form a crust that keeps water out, so sprinkle lightly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dried grounds in a bowl in the fridge can absorb smells. Some people use them as a gentle scrub for pots, or even for hands after chopping garlic.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Coffee hands instead of garlic hands. Sold.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fair trade. Just let them dry out first if you store them, damp grounds go mouldy quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I tried Vietnamese iced coffee on holiday and I've been dreaming about it since.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's so good. The classic version uses strong dark roast coffee, sweetened condensed milk and lots of ice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They had this little metal thing / on top of the glass.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a phin, a small drip filter. You put the coffee in, press it down gently, add hot water, and it slowly drips into the glass.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I make it without the filter?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, use very strong coffee from a moka pot or a French press. Stir it into the condensed milk while it's hot, then pour over ice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much condensed milk?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Start with a couple of tablespoons and adjust. It's meant to be sweet, but you can go lighter. A phin is cheap though, worth getting for the full experience.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Every day at three I crash and grab another coffee. Then I can't sleep. It's a stupid cycle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a very common cycle, not a stupid one. That afternoon dip is partly natural, your body clock dips after lunch.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So what am I supposed to do instead?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A short walk outside, ideally in daylight, gives a surprising lift. So does a big glass of cold water, since mild dehydration makes the slump worse.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A walk. Groundbreaking.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, I know it sounds boring. But ten minutes outside often works as well as half a coffee, without wrecking your sleep.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I / really, really need caffeine?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then try a small green tea or a half decaf coffee. Less caffeine, still a little boost, and kinder to your bedtime.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it possible to roast coffee beans at home? I keep seeing green beans for sale.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is, and it's a fun hobby. You can start with a heavy pan on the stove or a cheap popcorn popper.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: A popcorn popper? Really?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Really. The hot air keeps the beans moving so they roast evenly. Just do it outside or near an open window, there's a lot of smoke and chaff.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I know / when they're done?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Listen for the first crack, a popping sound like popcorn. Stopping shortly after gives a light roast, and keeping going towards a second crack gets darker.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I drink them straight away?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's best to let them rest for a day or two. Fresh roasted beans release a lot of gas, and the flavour settles after a short rest.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The bag says notes of chocolate, cherry and almond. I just taste coffee. Am I broken?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely not. Those notes are subtle hints, not added flavours. Most people need a bit of practice to pick them out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So it's a bit of / a marketing gimmick?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Partly description, partly a guide. The beans really do have different flavour compounds, but the words are the roaster's best attempt to describe them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I practise?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Taste two very different coffees side by side, like a light African roast and a dark Brazilian one. Differences jump out much more when you compare.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And let it cool?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, good instinct. Flavours often get clearer as the coffee cools a bit. Very hot coffee mostly just tastes hot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My coworker puts butter in his coffee and says it's the secret to productivity. Is that a thing?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It's a trend, often called butter coffee. People blend coffee with butter and sometimes coconut oil.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Does it actually do anything?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The fat makes it more filling, so some people feel steady energy without wanting breakfast. But there isn't strong evidence that it boosts focus.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It sounds like / a lot of calories.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be, often as much as a small meal. If it replaces breakfast, fine, but on top of breakfast it adds up quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I try it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you're curious, try it once with a small amount. Blend it well, otherwise you just get an oily layer on top.

option_sets.lead_in: I want to start making better coffee at home, and I've got a few choices.
options: The first one is a French press, cheap and simple, but you have to clean out the grounds.
Then there's a pour over cone, which makes a really clean cup but takes some practice.
Option three is a pod machine, super fast and easy, but the pods add up over time.
And the last one is an espresso machine with a milk steamer, which is pretty expensive.
moshi_comment: If you love lattes, the espresso machine is the only one that really gets you there, but it's a big investment. For plain black coffee, the French press or pour over give great flavor for little money. The pod machine wins on convenience but not taste.
Do you usually drink your coffee black or with milk? If it's black, I'd start with the pour over, it's cheap and rewarding. If you want milk drinks, the espresso machine is worth saving for.

option_sets.lead_in: I can't figure out which coffee beans to order for the office.
options: One is a dark roast that's bold and smoky, the kind most people expect from office coffee.
Another is a light roast from a small farm, fruity and bright, but some people find it sour.
Or we could get a medium blend that's smooth and balanced and a bit cheaper by the pound.
moshi_comment: For a whole office, the medium blend is the safest choice, it pleases most people and saves money. The dark roast is good if your coworkers like it strong with milk. The light roast is lovely but might get complaints.
Do people mostly drink it with milk and sugar? If so, the dark roast holds up better. If not, the medium blend is a nice middle ground.

option_sets.lead_in: My partner and I are buying our first proper coffee machine together, and we can't agree.
options: He wants a manual espresso machine with a steam wand, a bit fiddly but very satisfying.
I'd prefer a bean to cup machine that grinds and brews with one button.
There's also a filter machine with a timer, so coffee's ready when the alarm goes off.
Or we keep our cheap French press and spend the money on really good beans.
moshi_comment: The manual espresso machine is great if he enjoys the ritual, but it takes practice. The bean to cup is the easy everyday option. The timed filter is lovely for slow mornings, and better beans in the French press is the budget winner.

It depends on your mornings. If you're rushed, the bean to cup or the timed filter make life easy. The manual machine suits a hobbyist, and honestly, great beans in your French press might surprise you both.

option_sets.lead_in: My cafe needs a new plant milk option, and the supplier offered a few.
options: Oat milk is the most popular, foams beautifully and tastes a bit sweet.
Almond milk is lighter and nutty, but it can split in hot coffee.
Soy is cheap and creamy, though some customers say it tastes beany.
And there's a coconut milk blend that's great in iced drinks but strong tasting.
moshi_comment: Oat is the safe bet, people know it and it steams well. Almond and soy each have fans, but almond can split. Coconut is fun for a summer menu rather than an everyday choice.
I'd make oat your main one and maybe keep soy as a cheaper second. Almond is tricky in hot drinks, and coconut is best saved for iced specials.

option_sets.lead_in: I'm visiting a new city for one morning and I've found three cafes I want to try.
options: A tiny specialty roaster near the station that only does pour overs, standing room only.
A big old fashioned coffee house with chandeliers, cakes and waiters in waistcoats.
Or a little rooftop place with a view over the river, but it's a twenty minute walk uphill.
moshi_comment: If you love coffee itself, the roaster is the one, though you'll be standing. The coffee house is about the atmosphere and the cake. The rooftop is the most memorable view, if you don't mind the climb.

For one morning, I'd pick based on what you'll remember. The grand coffee house is a real experience, the roaster is best for the actual cup, and the rooftop wins on scenery. Could you grab a pour over at the station and then walk up for the view?

option_sets.lead_in: I'm trying to cut down on caffeine, and I've got a few ideas about how.
options: I could switch my afternoon cup to decaf and keep the morning one normal.
Another idea is half caf, mixing regular and decaf beans for every cup.
Or swap coffee for green tea, which has less caffeine but still gives a little lift.
moshi_comment: Switching the afternoon cup to decaf is the easiest, and it helps sleep the most. Half caf is a gentle way to cut back across the whole day. Green tea works if you're happy with a different drink entirely.
I'd start with the afternoon decaf, it's a small change with a big effect. Half caf is nice if you drink many cups, and green tea is a good fit if you're open to change.
